claim: The flight muscles, dorsal air sacs, wing blades, and thoracic cuticle of the Drosophila adult function in concert.
source: The flight muscles, dorsal air sacs, wing blades, and thoracic cuticle of the Drosophila adult function in concert, and their progenitor cells develop together in the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about Drosophila anatomy and development.

claim: Progenitor cells of flight muscles, dorsal air sacs, wing blades, and thoracic cuticle develop together in the wing imaginal disc.

claim: The wing disc orchestrates dorsal air sac development by producing decapentaplegic and fibroblast growth factor.
source: The wing disc orchestrates dorsal air sac development by producing decapentaplegic and fibroblast growth factor that travel via specific cytonemes in order to signal to the air sac primordium (ASP).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior work from the lab.

claim: Decapentaplegic and fibroblast growth factor travel via specific cytonemes to signal to the air sac primordium.
source: The wing disc orchestrates dorsal air sac development by producing decapentaplegic and fibroblast growth factor that travel via specific cytonemes in order to signal to the air sac primordium (ASP).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior work from the lab.

claim: Cytonemes link flight muscle progenitors (myoblasts) to disc cells.
source: Here, we report that cytonemes also link flight muscle progenitors (myoblasts) to disc cells and to the ASP, enabling myoblasts to relay signaling between the disc and the ASP.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by GRASP experiments and imaging data shown in Figures 2 and 11.

claim: Cytonemes link myoblasts to the ASP.
source: Here, we report that cytonemes also link flight muscle progenitors (myoblasts) to disc cells and to the ASP, enabling myoblasts to relay signaling between the disc and the ASP.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by GRASP experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Myoblasts relay signaling between the disc and the ASP.
source: Here, we report that cytonemes also link flight muscle progenitors (myoblasts) to disc cells and to the ASP, enabling myoblasts to relay signaling between the disc and the ASP.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by genetic and imaging experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Frizzled-containing myoblast cytonemes take up Wingless from the disc.
source: Frizzled (Fz)-containing myoblast cytonemes take up Wingless (Wg) from the disc, and Delta (Dl)-containing myoblast cytonemes contribute to Notch activation in the ASP.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figure 11 showing Fz:Cherry in myoblast cytonemes and Wg:Cherry uptake.

claim: Delta-containing myoblast cytonemes contribute to Notch activation in the ASP.
source: Frizzled (Fz)-containing myoblast cytonemes take up Wingless (Wg) from the disc, and Delta (Dl)-containing myoblast cytonemes contribute to Notch activation in the ASP.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figures 4-5 showing Dl:RFP in myoblast cytonemes and genetic experiments showing effects on Notch signaling.

claim: Wg signaling negatively regulates Dl expression in the myoblasts.
source: Wg signaling negatively regulates Dl expression in the myoblasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by genetic experiments in Figure 8 showing increased Dl in dsh mutant clones and TCFDN expression.

claim: The air sac primordium depends on Branchless/FGF and Dpp signaling proteins that the wing disc produces.
source: Previous studies from this lab showed that the air sac primordium (ASP), which is the progenitor of the dorsal air sacs, depends on Branchless/FGF (FGF) and Dpp signaling proteins that the wing disc produces (Sato and Kornberg, 2002; Roy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The wing disc can be described as a flattened sac that juxtaposes the apical surfaces of two connected epithelial sheets across a narrow lumen.
source: The wing disc can be described as a flattened sac that juxtaposes the apical surfaces of two connected epithelial sheets across a narrow lumen.
evidence: This is a description of wing disc anatomy stated in the introduction.

claim: The columnar epithelium generates the wing blade and most of the notum.
source: One of the sheets, called the columnar epithelium because its cells are highly elongated along their apical/basal axis, generates the wing blade and most of the notum, the dorsal cuticle of the thorax.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about wing disc development.

claim: The wing disc is encapsulated by a basement membrane.
source: The wing disc is encapsulated by a basement membrane, but a branch of the tracheal system (the transverse connective) penetrates the basement membrane at several sites in the dorsal region of the disc (Guha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: A branch of the tracheal system (the transverse connective) penetrates the basement membrane at several sites in the dorsal region of the disc.
source: The wing disc is encapsulated by a basement membrane, but a branch of the tracheal system (the transverse connective) penetrates the basement membrane at several sites in the dorsal region of the disc (Guha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: During the third instar (L3), the transverse connective sprouts a tubular outgrowth—the ASP—in response to FGF expressed by a group of nearby columnar epithelial cells.
source: Transverse connective that is within the basement membrane lies adjacent to the basal surface of the columnar epithelium, and during the third instar (L3), this segment of the transverse connective sprouts a tubular outgrowth—the ASP—in response to FGF expressed by a group of nearby columnar epithelial cells (Sato and Kornberg, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Myoblasts that are the progenitors of the flight muscles are at the basal surface of the columnar epithelium, underneath the basement membrane, and in the vicinity of the tracheal branches.
source: Myoblasts that are the progenitors of the flight muscles are also at the basal surface of the columnar epithelium, underneath the basement membrane, and in the vicinity of the tracheal branches.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about myoblast location.

claim: Myoblasts proliferate during L3 to extend over most of the dorsal part of the disc where the cells that will produce the notum cuticle grow.
source: They proliferate during L3 to extend over most of the dorsal part of the disc where the cells that will produce the notum cuticle grow (Sudarsan et al., 2001; Gunage et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Notch, Dpp, and Wg signaling proteins contribute to the growth and diversification of the cells of the wing disc.
source: Signaling proteins that contribute to the growth and diversification of the cells of the wing disc have been extensively characterized. Three that are relevant to the ASP and myoblasts are Notch, Dpp, and Wg (Couso et al., 1995; Ng et al., 1996; Brennan et al., 1999; Steneberg et al., 1999; Sudarsan et al., 2001; Baena-Lopez et al., 2003; Giraldez and Cohen, 2003; Marois et al., 2006; Herranz et al., 2008; Gunage et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Notch signaling has essential roles at both the dorsal/ventral and anterior/posterior compartment borders of the disc.
source: Notch signaling has essential roles at both the dorsal/ventral and anterior/posterior compartment borders of the disc, and although it has been shown to specify fusion cell fate and branch identity during formation of tracheal system in the embryo, a role in larval trachea has not been reported.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about Notch signaling.

claim: Notch signaling specifies fusion cell fate and branch identity during formation of tracheal system in the embryo.
source: Notch signaling has essential roles at both the dorsal/ventral and anterior/posterior compartment borders of the disc, and although it has been shown to specify fusion cell fate and branch identity during formation of tracheal system in the embryo, a role in larval trachea has not been reported.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: A role for Notch signaling in larval trachea has not been reported.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction to highlight the novelty of the current findings.

claim: Dpp-expressing cells line the anterior side of the anterior/posterior compartment border at all stages of L3 discs.
source: Dpp-expressing cells line the anterior side of the anterior/posterior compartment border at all stages of L3 discs, and Dpp that is produced near the ASP activates Dpp signal transduction in the ASP that is necessary for its morphogenesis.

claim: Dpp that is produced near the ASP activates Dpp signal transduction in the ASP that is necessary for its morphogenesis.
source: Dpp-expressing cells line the anterior side of the anterior/posterior compartment border at all stages of L3 discs, and Dpp that is produced near the ASP activates Dpp signal transduction in the ASP that is necessary for its morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

source: ASP cells express the Dpp receptor but do not express Dpp.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

source: The mechanism by which Dpp signals from disc cells to the ASP involves exchange of Dpp between producing and receiving cells at synapses that form where cytonemes link ASP cells to Dpp-producing disc cells (Roy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

source: ASP cytonemes that contain the Dpp receptor have been observed extending as far as 40 μm, crossing over approximately 15–20 disc cells to reach sources of Dpp.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a prior observation.

claim: ASP cytonemes transport Dpp from producing cells to the ASP.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Dpp signal transduction is dependent on the contacts cytonemes make with the disc cells.
source: These cytonemes transport Dpp from producing cells to the ASP, and signal transduction is dependent on the contacts they make with the disc cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Comparably long ASP cytonemes containing the FGF receptor have been observed reaching FGF-expressing disc cells.
source: Comparably long ASP cytonemes containing the FGF receptor have been observed reaching FGF-expressing disc cells, and in the wing disc, Hh dispersion is effected by a similar mechanism (Callejo et al., 2011; Bischoff et al., 2013).

claim: In the wing disc, Hh dispersion is effected by a cytoneme-mediated mechanism.
source: Comparably long ASP cytonemes containing the FGF receptor have been observed reaching FGF-expressing disc cells, and in the wing disc, Hh dispersion is effected by a similar mechanism (Callejo et al., 2011; Bischoff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The evidence that Dpp, FGF, and Hh paracrine signaling are mediated by cytonemes is strong.
source: In these contexts, the evidence that Dpp, FGF, and Hh paracrine signaling are mediated by cytonemes is strong.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of prior work.

claim: Expression patterns of Wg change throughout the L3.
source: Expression patterns of Wg change throughout the L3.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

source: In the wing blade primordium, Wg is expressed broadly in early L3 discs, but in late L3 discs, it is expressed in well-delineated bands both at the dorsal/ventral compartment border and around the periphery (Phillips and Whittle, 1993; Couso et al., 1995; Strigini and Cohen, 2000; Alexandre et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In late L3 discs, Wg is expressed in well-delineated bands both at the dorsal/ventral compartment border and around the periphery.

source: Wg is also expressed in the notum primordium where it has a role in myoblast proliferation and diversification (Sudarsan et al., 2001; Gunage et al., 2014).

source: The mechanism by which Wg signals from the disc cells to myoblasts has not been studied.

claim: It is not known how signaling by tethered Wg is related to the normal processes that present wild type Wg to receiving cells.
source: In wing discs, a mutant form of Wg that is tethered to the plasma membrane by a heterologous transmembrane domain is active (Alexandre et al., 2014), but it is not known how signaling by this tethered form is related to the normal processes that present wild type Wg to receiving cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction to highlight a gap in knowledge.

claim: There is no experimental evidence that shows directly that Wg disperses by passive diffusion or that it signals in vivo as a soluble, free protein.

source: Images of the mid-dorsal region of early, mid, and late L3 discs revealed the expansion of the myoblasts and growth of the ASP as well as the close proximity of the trachea and myoblasts (Figure 1A–C).

claim: GFP reconstitution across synaptic partners (GRASP) monitors the interaction of two non-fluorescent fragments of GFP (GFP1–10 and GFP11) that are expressed separately as external, membrane-tethered proteins on different cells.
source: To investigate whether the ASP, myoblasts, and disc cells contact each other directly, we applied the GFP reconstitution across synaptic partners (GRASP) technique (Feinberg et al., 2008). This method monitors the interaction of two non-fluorescent fragments of GFP (GFP1–10 and GFP11) that are expressed separately as external, membrane-tethered proteins on different cells; reconstitution of GFP by fragments present on cells that juxtapose at <100 nm generates green fluorescence.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Reconstitution of GFP by fragments present on cells that juxtapose at <100 nm generates green fluorescence.
source: This method monitors the interaction of two non-fluorescent fragments of GFP (GFP1–10 and GFP11) that are expressed separately as external, membrane-tethered proteins on different cells; reconstitution of GFP by fragments present on cells that juxtapose at <100 nm generates green fluorescence.

claim: Myoblasts with reduced diaRNA had fewer cytonemes.
source: To investigate whether the IFP-marked, Dl-containing cytonemes function in Notch signaling, we genetically ablated myoblast cytonemes by inactivating diaphanous (dia) and neuroglian (nrg). The Dia protein is a formin whose activated form localizes to tips of filopodia (Homem and Peifer, 2008; Rousso et al., 2013) and cytonemes (Roy et al., 2014), and Nrg is an L1-type cell adhesion protein that has been implicated in the development and stability of neuronal synapses (Enneking et al., 2013). Loss-of-function phenotypes are dependent on context and degree of knockdown and negative results are uninformative, but it has been reported that Dia and Nrg are necessary for cytoneme-mediated Dpp signaling in the ASP (Roy et al., 2014). We examined the effects of diaRNAi and nrgRNAi expression on myoblast cytonemes and on Notch signaling in the ASP and found that both the relative number of myoblast cytonemes and Notch signal transduction in the ASP were reduced (Figure 5D–L).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5D-L.
